summary: Round 2, test review. All four round-1 majors are CLOSED, each verified by re-running the mutation on this tree with a clean :sequencer:build: (1) Faults.none() inside CommitProtocolSimulation.run now fails aROUGHRun on faults().isNotEmpty(); (2) disabling CommitLog.commit's fail-closed-on-SEAL now fails aCleanRunViolatesNothing with an I5 violation -- clean seed 7 makes NINE zombie attempts, measured -- and deleting the zombie list fails zombieAttempts().isPositive(); (3) putIfMatch's ambiguous branch throwing without landing fails anAmbiguousPutIfMatchALSOLands; (4) deleting the I1 arm fails aSequenceAPPEARINGTWICE. LocalSequencer's open(prevEpoch, 0) -- round-1 F1 -- now dies in the simulation AND in InvariantsTest, and it dies through the I2 arm INDEPENDENTLY of checkLink (verified by deleting checkLink and re-running the production mutation: the checker still reports I2). SimulatedClock.advance as a no-op dies; unseeding any of the three fault streams dies; duplicatePut clobbering with put dies; injected() returning empty dies; inheritedOffsets returning empty, dropping its recursion, or off-by-one on the high-water all die. What remains are minors, all in the checker's secondary arms plus two brittleness/overclaim findings on the ROUGH seed. Nothing blocks: no existing assertion was weakened (every source file in the diff is new), no sleep, socket, fixed port or system temp, tier is T1 on MemoryBinStore throughout.

findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED (clean build, full :sequencer:test green): the I2 boundary is unpinned. `if (run.firstOffset() < from)` -> `if (run.firstOffset() < from - 1)` survives every test. The only I2 fixture (InvariantsTest.java:288) overlaps by TWO records -- delta 1 assigns 0..4, delta 2 claims 3..5 -- so 3 < 4 is still true and the violation is still reported. A reassignment of exactly ONE record is invisible to the mutated predicate and no test notices. That is the shape a boundary off-by-one produces, and it is the one M4.6e's crossing is most likely to get wrong: note that the CHECKER's own off-by-one (lastOffset()+1 -> lastOffset(), Invariants.java:221) DIES, so the machinery is pinned while the predicate's boundary is not. A fixture that overlaps by exactly one record closes it.
findings.failure_scenario: Someone tidies the I2 arm -- swapping `<` for `<=`, or 'fixing' what looks like an off-by-one after reading the neighbouring lastOffset()+1 -- and the arm stops reporting single-record reassignments. M4.13 then runs 1,000 seeds and reports 'I1-I5 hold' while the most likely real I2 defect at a chain boundary, a successor resuming one offset early, is not something the checker can see.

findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED: checkLink's fork arm is deletable. `if (closing.continuedAt() != epoch)` -> `if (false)` survives the whole suite on a clean build. Both other arms have fixtures (aCONTINUENamingAChainNobodySEALED pins `closing == null`, aCONTINUEThatMISSTATES pins the prevSeq arm) but the middle one -- the ONLY arm that detects a FORK, i.e. two chains continuing from one predecessor whose SEAL names just one of them -- has none. This is the same class as round-1's I1 finding, arriving in the code that was added to FIX round-1's F1. Mitigating, and why this is minor rather than major: production's seal target is independently pinned by four exact-Seal assertions in LocalSequencerTest, verified -- mutating LocalSequencer to seal(epoch + 1) kills seven tests including this arm firing in the simulation.
findings.failure_scenario: The arm is deleted or its comparison drifts (`!= epoch` against the wrong side of the join). A chain that continues from a predecessor sealed FOR SOMEBODY ELSE -- the live fork the whole seal protocol exists to prevent -- then produces no `link` violation, and the checker's javadoc claim that 'a chain may only continue from one that was sealed for it' is established by nothing.

findings.summary: TWO SURVIVING MUTATIONS, MEASURED: the 'folded to the predecessor's own SEAL' logic that the comment at :210-213 calls the point is unconstrained. (a) `upTo = s.sequence()` -> `upTo = Long.MAX_VALUE` survives. (b) deleting `if (e.sequence() > upTo) { break; }` at :216-218 survives. Either makes the checker fold a fenced leader's post-seal entries into the successor's inherited history. Direction matters and is why this is minor: both mutants make the checker STRICTER (inherited high-water too high -> spurious `gap` reports), so the risk is false alarms rather than missed violations. But nothing pins the boundary either way, and no fixture builds a predecessor with entries past its SEAL and a successor inheriting from it.
findings.failure_scenario: A refactor drops the seal bound (it is easy to read as redundant, since the per-chain walk already reports I5 for those entries). M4.13's sweep then starts reporting `gap` violations on any seed where a fenced leader landed a write before it was refused, and the noise is either chased as a protocol defect or -- worse -- the offending arm is loosened to silence it.

findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED: the offset-`gap` arm is deletable. `} else if (run.firstOffset() > from) {` -> `} else if (false) {` survives the whole suite. No test asserts a `gap` violation is ever PRODUCED -- aHOLEInTheChain (InvariantsTest.java:306) asserts `chain`, which is the sequence-number gap, a different arm. Yet the offset-gap arm is what carries several other kills: it is the violation that fails aCleanRunViolatesNothing when inheritedOffsets is mutated to return an empty map, and when the recursion is removed. So a detector doing real work in the kill set has no fixture of its own, and deleting it would silently un-kill those two mutants.
findings.failure_scenario: The `gap` arm is deleted as 'not one of I1-I5'. A severed CONTINUE that makes a successor resume ABOVE the high-water mark -- data loss, NFR-11 -- then produces no violation at all, and the two inheritance mutants that this arm currently kills become survivors without any test changing.

findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED: the never-opened step-over loop is dead in the current test set. Deleting `while (from >= 1 && neverOpened(prior)) { ... }` (:196-199) survives the whole suite on a clean build, and `neverOpened` (:269) is only pinned in one direction (returning always-true degenerates into the already-killed empty-inherited mutant). Nothing in the diff builds a chain abandoned before its CONTINUE was written. Coupled to the next finding: the only run that produces burned epochs is the ROUGH one -- measured, ROUGH seeds burn ~100 epochs per 120 rounds for ~4 takeovers -- and its violations() is asserted by nothing, so the subsystem is unreachable from any assertion.
findings.failure_scenario: The loop is deleted as unreachable-looking code. Every chain whose leader acquired and died before writing its CONTINUE then breaks the ancestry walk, so a successor inherits nothing and the checker reports a `gap` for every stream on any seed with a burned epoch -- which under faults is most of them. M4.13's 1,000-seed sweep drowns in false violations, or the arm that reports them is loosened.

findings.summary: THE FAULTED RUN'S INVARIANTS ARE ASSERTED BY NOTHING. aROUGHRun asserts faults(), the three fault kinds, zombieAttempts and zombieWrites -- but never violations(). Only the CLEAN run (line 46) checks the chain. So the store that exists to inject faults never has its output checked against I1/I2/I5, which is the milestone's whole claim. MEASURED, and this is NOT the gap the backlog row defers (the row defers the faulted-run PROGRESS assertions and the seed range, both of which do fail today): I probed ROUGH (0.05, 0.05, 0.1) over seeds 0-30 and EVERY seed reports viol=0, so `assertThat(result.violations()).isEmpty()` passes today at seed 9 and everywhere near it. One line. It would also be the only assertion that reaches the burned-epoch / never-opened path of the previous finding, since faults are what burns epochs.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13 lands the 1,000-seed sweep on top of this harness and reports 'I1-I5 hold'. The checker has never once been run under injected faults with its output asserted, so any invariant the fault classes reach -- and unreachable/ambiguousPut/duplicatePut are exactly the classes that reach them -- is established by the clean path only. The fault decorator is proved to FIRE (round-1's fix) without ever being proved to have its consequences CHECKED.

findings.summary: `zombieWrites().isZero()` IS A TRACE PIN, NOT A BARRIER CHECK, and its `as(...)` description -- 'and every one of them was refused -- the seal barrier held' -- overclaims. Two measurements. (a) It does not kill the barrier mutation: with CommitLog.commit's `if (taken instanceof Seal seal) throw fenced(seal)` disabled on a clean build, aROUGHRun stays GREEN; the kill comes from aCleanRunViolatesNothing (I5 at sequence 7) and from CommitLogTest. (b) At the same ROUGH probabilities, seed 5 yields zombieWrites=1 -- a fenced writer DOES land a write today -- so 'the barrier held' is a property of seed 9's trace, not of the system under faults. The comment is the kind of prose this repo's review record is built out of, so the mismatch matters more than a bare assertion would.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader (or M4.16's author) takes the line at its word and believes the fenced-write path is proved safe under faults. It is not: an adjacent seed under identical configuration lands a fenced write, and nothing in this file would report it, because the same test asserts no violations. Meanwhile any harness change that shifts the draw order can flip seed 9 to zombieWrites=1 and the test goes red for a reason nobody can attribute to a defect.

findings.summary: SEED 9 IS LOAD-BEARING AND MARGINAL, AND THE COMMENT NAMES THE WRONG SEED. Measured over ROUGH seeds 0-30: 20 of 31 give zombieAttempts == 0; the rest give 1; seed 9 gives 2, the maximum in the range. So the anti-vacuity assertion sits on the thinnest margin available. It fails LOUD rather than going silently vacuous, which is the right direction and why this is minor -- demonstrated: unseeding one of the three fault streams took seed 9 to zombieAttempts=0 and this exact assertion failed, for a reason unrelated to any protocol defect. Two concrete fixes: the CLEAN run at seed 7 measures NINE zombie attempts (an order of magnitude of headroom) so the zombie assertion belongs there or in addition there; and the comment at line 84 says 'Seed 22 drives fenced writers at the chain' while the test runs seed 9 -- seed 22 measures zombieAttempts == 0.
findings.failure_scenario: Any change to the harness's draw order -- a fourth fault class, a reordered branch, a different pods/rounds default -- re-rolls seed 9 and this test goes red with a message about fenced leaders that has nothing to do with the change. The likely response is to hunt for a new seed, which re-establishes the same margin, or to drop the assertion, which re-opens round-1's finding 2 verbatim.

findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED: the Faults probability guard is unconstrained. `if (!(p >= 0.0 && p <= 1.0))` -> `if (false)` survives the whole suite on a clean build. No test constructs an out-of-range probability. Its own seven-line javadoc (:138-146) calls it 'rung 1 of gate-design' and names the exact failure it exists to prevent: a negative probability disables its class silently, because `fires` tests `draws.nextDouble() < p`, while injected() still shows the other classes firing -- so an aggregate 'faults fired' assertion stays green over a sweep that never exercised the class it was written for. Three assertThatThrownBy lines close it.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13 needs per-class seeds and someone parameterises the probabilities from a sweep table or a system property. A typo or a unit slip (5 for '5%') then passes construction: >1 fires always and <0 fires never, and the class that never fires is invisible because criterion 1's evidence is drawn from injected(), which shows the other two.

findings.summary: theCheckerSAYSItNowEXAMINESTheBoundaryBetweenChains asserts a hard-coded constant. Invariants.crossEpochOffsetsChecked() is `return true` with no derivation, so the only mutation the test can kill is editing that literal. MEASURED that this is not hypothetical: I deleted the seal-bounded inherited fold (upTo -> Long.MAX_VALUE, and the break past it) and the never-opened step-over -- all of them boundary examination -- and this test stayed green while the flag went on reporting `true`. The test's own comment says the flag exists 'so that claim is in the API rather than in a comment'; as written it is a comment with an assertion around it.
findings.failure_scenario: Boundary checking is weakened or removed in Invariants -- three separate ways of doing that survive the suite today -- and the flag keeps saying the boundary is examined. A caller that reports 'clean, and the boundary was checked' on the strength of the flag is then reporting safety nothing established, which is the exact failure the flag was introduced to prevent.

findings.summary: ROUND-1 MINOR NOT CLOSED: java.time.Clock.systemUTC() is still used at InvariantsTest.java:60 and :154 (the `start` helper), in the same package as the new SimulatedClock this diff adds. Not load-bearing today, and that is checked: the TTL is 10s and both takeovers happen through close()/release rather than through expiry, so nothing waits on the clock. But testing.md rule 1 and non-negotiable 7 say a T1 test injects the seam, and the seam is now sitting next to the file.
findings.failure_scenario: Someone extends one of these fixtures to cover a lapsed lease (the natural next step for the takeover fixture) and reaches for a sleep or a short TTL because the clock in front of them is a wall clock. The test then becomes the flake the whole SimulatedClock exists to avoid, and the file that introduced the fix is the file that did not use it.
